strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear identification of under-exploration and under-exploitation inefficiencies in GRPO
Mathematically grounded hierarchical rollout planning using Student's t-confidence intervals that satisfies three desirable criteria
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 datasets with thorough ablations and sensitivity analysis
Significant practical gains: 2.7× faster training convergence and 13.6% response length reduction
Good reproducibility support including Algorithm 1, hyperparameter specifications, implementation details, and ICL prompt template
Demonstrated compatibility with existing methods (GSPO) suggesting modularity and complementary benefits
weaknesses: Improvements on reasoning models are modest: +1.4% pass@1 and +2.5% cons@32 for Qwen3-1.7B, contradicting abstract claims of 'up to 4% pass@1'

Theoretical justification lacking for key design choices: uncertainty reduction approximation (Eq. 2) lacks derivation, novelty measure exponential transformation (Eq. 5) alternatives unexplored, phase allocation appears arbitrary
ICL seeding component underdeveloped theoretically and practically: corpus size constraints unclear, growth dynamics unspecified, failure modes unanalyzed
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported; single-run results raise concerns about reliability of improvements
Incomplete ablations: missing analysis on phase counts/ratios, no direct comparison with cited baselines (TreeRL, DAPO), error analysis of failure modes absent
Implementation clarity gaps: ICL corpus initialization details vague, similarity computation unexplained, stability of variance estimates with only 4 base rollouts questionable
Novelty primarily combinatorial: uncertainty-driven sampling and novelty bonuses exist in RL literature; main contribution is integration rather than fundamental innovation
Misleading framing: abstract overstates improvements compared to Table 1 results; appendix examples are anecdotal without systematic quality comparison

strengths: Clear problem motivation identifying genuine GRPO limitations in rollout allocation and sparse rewards
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 datasets and 2 model scales with thorough ablations and sensitivity analysis
Consistent empirical improvements: 1-4% pass@1 gains, up to 6% cons@32, and 2.7× training convergence speedup
Detailed ablation study (Figure 3b) demonstrating each component's contribution to overall performance
Strong empirical analysis with informative breakdowns of inference efficiency, ICL success rates, and completion metrics
Well-written paper with clear exposition of motivation and method
weaknesses: Weak theoretical justification for core design choices: Student's t-confidence interval, exploration bonus functional form φ_q(T,n_q)=λ√log(1+T)/n_q, and phased allocation strategy lack principled derivation or formal optimization framework

Limited novelty in components: ICL seeding is standard prompt engineering; claiming 'first demonstration of ICL within RL' overstates contribution. Novelty measure (Eq. 5) lacks justification for exponential form and why sequence likelihood is appropriate
Experimental fairness concerns: No confirmation that GRPO/GSPO baselines use identical computational budgets; no statistical significance testing or error bars; no multiple runs reported

Modest effect sizes for added complexity: 1.4% average pass@1 improvement over GSPO and 2.5% cons@32 are incremental gains. Hyperparameter sensitivity (Table 2 shows ±1.07 variance) raises stability questions

Incomplete mechanism analysis: No analysis of zero-reward prompt prevalence or whether they're actual bottleneck; Figure 3c shows XRPO+GSPO sometimes outperforms XRPO alone without adequate explanation; cherry-picked examples in appendix
Unjustified hyperparameter complexity: Multiple parameters (λ, λ_novelty, κ_clip, n_base, N_plan) with incomplete sensitivity analysis; no guidance for hyperparameter selection in new domains

Limited scope and generalization: Only evaluated on math/coding tasks with Qwen models; relies on proprietary Qwen3-Embedding-8B reducing reproducibility; unknown transfer to other model families and task domains
Critical ICL implementation details missing: Corpus initialization/growth analysis absent; similarity metric unspecified; unclear when corpus helps vs. hurts; corpus update rule vague
Algorithm clarity issues: Line 6 of Algorithm 1 unclear on SQ contents; notation inconsistency (A+ vs A'); corpus update rule underspecified
Reproducibility concerns: Exact dataset versions not specified; ICL corpus construction incomplete; embedding similarity details missing; no code availability mentioned

strengths: Well-motivated work addressing genuine bottlenecks in RLVR training (slow convergence, sparse rewards, hard prompts)
Mathematically grounded uncertainty-based rollout allocation using Student's t-confidence intervals
Comprehensive experimental validation across 7 diverse benchmarks with consistent improvements (1.4-2.5% on reasoning models, up to 20% on non-reasoning models)
Strong practical benefits: 2.4-2.7× faster training convergence and 13-14% shorter inference sequences
Novel application of ICL seeding within RLVR to break zero-reward symmetry, with demonstrated 4-10% recovery on hard prompts
Thorough ablation studies and sensitivity analysis demonstrating each component's contribution and robustness
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and comprehensive algorithm description
Demonstrated compatibility with recent state-of-the-art methods (GSPO)
weaknesses: Improvements over GSPO are incremental (1-2.5% on reasoning models where baselines are already competitive) rather than transformative
Limited theoretical novelty: each component (uncertainty sampling, ICL, entropy bonuses) relies on established techniques; their combination lacks deep integration insights
Experimental scope limited to Qwen models only; no evaluation on LLaMA, Mistral, or other mainstream LLM families
Design choices lack strong justification: why Student's t-distribution? Why the specific φ_q = λ√(log(1+T))/n_q formula? Why K=2 examples for ICL?
ICL seeding limitations underexplored: only 6-10% success rate on hard prompts; effectiveness on truly OOD problems unclear; requires embedding model dependency (Qwen3-Embedding-8B)
Technical details need clarification: Eq. 2 approximation assumes smooth behavior potentially problematic for small n_q; novelty measure relationship to entropy remains informal
Missing key comparisons with related methods (TreeRL, TreeRPO explicitly mentioned in related work)
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for reported improvements
Computational cost analysis missing despite claims of 'lightweight implementation'; high GPU requirements (16×H200) limit reproducibility and accessibility
Limited ablation scope: hyperparameter sensitivity only varies λ_novelty and κ_clip, not n_base, T, or λ (exploration weight)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B) and datasets with extensive ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution
Strong practical results: 2.4-2.7× convergence speedup with only 4.7% per-step overhead, and consistent 1-4% accuracy improvements across benchmarks
Well-motivated problem formulation clearly identifying genuine limitations of GRPO (under-exploration and under-exploitation) with good exploration-exploitation lens
Solid experimental design including sensitivity analysis, ICL train/test ablation eliminating data leakage, and analysis of allocation non-uniformity (91.6% of rounds)
Clear presentation with detailed appendices covering truncation effects, latency analysis, and retrieval quality ablations enabling good reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: three established techniques (confidence-interval-based allocation, ICL for LLMs, entropy bonuses) combined incrementally; novelty score (Eq. 5) is simple exponential transformation of log-likelihood without strong justification

Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite modest improvements (1-4% typically); unclear baseline hyperparameter tuning effort and random seed specification

ICL seeding concerns: only applied during training not inference; distinction from data augmentation is semantic; corpus built exclusively from model's own solutions introduces bias; risks of distribution shift and non-stationarity inadequately discussed

Novelty-guided advantage sharpening lacks justification: functional form in Eq. 5 appears arbitrary; only applicable to binary rewards; clamping mechanism (Eq. 6) is ad-hoc; isolated contribution modest (3.5% degradation) and cannot distinguish error types

Hierarchical rollout planning under-motivated: phased allocation is ad-hoc; exploration bonus ϕ_q = λ log(1+T)/n_q lacks theoretical justification; sensitivity analysis only tests hyperparameters not the mechanism itself
Limited scope: only math and code generation tasks; models up to 7B (not 300B+); unclear scalability and generalization to diverse domains

Missing critical analyses: no ablation on ICL corpus size/update frequency; no analysis of learned reasoning strategies; failure case analysis absent; post-hoc validation of no-length-bias claim leaves subtle biases unclear

strengths: Clear problem motivation and comprehensive evaluation across multiple models and datasets with extensive ablations
Practical efficiency gains: 4% accuracy improvement with 2.7× convergence speedup and negligible per-step overhead (4.7%)
Principled uncertainty-based rollout allocation using t-distribution confidence intervals with mathematical grounding
Thorough supplementary analysis including hyperparameter sensitivity, ablations, and detailed training dynamics
weaknesses: Critical fairness issue: XRPO uses ICL seeding during training while baseline methods do not, creating an unequal experimental comparison. A fair comparison would require all methods trained on identical corpora.
Individual components lack novelty: uncertainty-based allocation applies classical statistics, ICL seeding is established, advantage sharpening extends existing entropy-based approaches incrementally

Questionable theoretical foundation: t-distribution confidence interval (Eq. 1) assumes normally distributed rewards but binary 0/1 verification rewards violate this assumption, undermining formal justification

Ad-hoc design choices without strong justification: exploration bonus ϕ_q = λ log(1+T)/n_q is hand-designed; novelty formula η_i = e^(s(y_i) - s̄) lacks motivation for exponential form; phased allocation strategy appears arbitrary

Weak evidence for ICL transfer learning: even random ICL provides benefits (+1.7% over no ICL, Table 11), suggesting improvements may stem from added context rather than sophisticated semantic transfer. Effectiveness demonstrated on DAPO training data, not held-out benchmarks.
Limited individual component contributions: advantage sharpening alone provides only ~3.5% improvement (Figure 3b); HRP produces non-uniform allocations in only 91.6% of training rounds (Appendix J)

Incomplete comparisons: missing evaluations against other curriculum learning methods (CurES vs. XRPO compared, but not E3-RL4LLMs, GVM-RAFT, etc.); no ablation of uncertainty-based vs. difficulty-based allocation on main benchmarks
Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; some improvements (1-2%) lack statistical validation; convergence speedup based on reaching specific thresholds

Limited scope and generalization: evaluation restricted to math reasoning and code generation; largest model 7B; acknowledged lack of evaluation on 300B+ parameter models; domain generalization unclear
Reproducibility concerns: reliance on proprietary embeddings (Qwen3-Embedding-8B) for ICL retrieval; many hyperparameters requiring tuning; implementation details incomplete; code not yet available

strengths: Clear problem motivation through exploration-exploitation framing with empirical validation of ICL effectiveness (Figure 2)
Principled mathematical design with Student's t-confidence intervals for uncertainty-based allocation (Eq. 1-3) and length-normalized novelty measures rigorously analyzed in appendices
Comprehensive experimental validation across 3 models (1.7B-7B) and 7 datasets with consistent improvements: 2.4-2.7× convergence speedup and 1.4% pass@1 gains
Thorough ablation studies isolating component contributions (Figure 3b, Table 5) with sensitivity analysis showing robustness (Table 4: ±1.1-1.4 std dev)
Practical efficiency with only 4.7% per-step overhead (Appendix B: theoretical analysis showing negligible overhead scales with batch size), compensated by faster convergence
Strong experimental methodology eliminating data leakage by evaluating without ICL corpus (§4.1), with non-uniform allocation in 91.6% of rounds validating exploration behavior (Appendix J)
Honest treatment of limitations (scope to small models, corpus bootstrapping concerns) and extensive supplementary analysis (truncation effects, retrieval quality, train/test ICL ablations)
weaknesses: Incremental algorithmic novelty: uncertainty-based allocation and novelty-based advantage shaping are straightforward applications of existing RL/statistical principles rather than fundamental innovations

ICL corpus exhibits potential circular dependency where hard problems may never generate successful rollouts to seed the corpus; paper lacks analysis of which problem types benefit most from seeding and how external teacher-generated examples would affect performance
Ablations show *that* each component helps but not *why* or *when*: missing characterization of which prompt categories benefit from HRP vs. ICL vs. AS, and how contributions vary across model scales

Limited scope undermines generalizability claims: models tested are small (max 7B); evaluation of larger 13B+ models would strengthen 'pushing limits' claims given acknowledged different scaling dynamics

Advantage sharpening design choices lack thorough justification: (i) boosting only reward=1 justified only by binary ORM limitation, (ii) exponential novelty function (e^(s(y_i)-s̄)) not compared to alternatives (linear/log), (iii) κ_clip=0.5 appears ad-hoc with sparse sensitivity analysis

Statistical rigor concerns: no confidence intervals or significance tests reported; with 32-candidate evaluation, variance quantification missing; some improvements modest (Llama AIME'25: 0.63% vs. 0.52%, Codeforces: 13.80 vs. 13.72 ~0.6%)
Comparison fairness: different methods' filtering/allocation strategies make direct comparison difficult; results with matched computational budgets across baselines would strengthen claims

Missing critical analyses: (i) no evaluation of dataset size scaling beyond 10K examples, (ii) no out-of-distribution prompt evaluation, (iii) no analysis of performance on easy vs. hard prompt subsets separately, (iv) limited exploration of ICL corpus corruption robustness
